messages.subject: Comparison of odds ratios across GLMMs
messages.subject_clean: Comparison of odds ratios across GLMMs
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I am using binomial GLMMs (random intercept models) to determine the influences on determiner omission in PPs in German. Examples are "ohne groessere Wanderung" (without bigger, i.e. longer hike), "mit blutiger Spritze" (with bloody syringe). According to the grammar of count nouns, we should always find a determiner here, i.e ohne *eine* groessere Wanderung, mit *einer* blutigen Spritze.

For the purposes of this question, I'll focus on the models for the prepositions *unter* (under) and *mit* (with). 

The GLMMs I am using consist of categorial features, i.e. factors, one of which is called nominal_dep_mod (aggregated nominal dependency). This factor describes possible extensions of the noun in the PP, i.e. complements and modifiers, such as postnominal genitives, PPs, relative clauses, and complement clauses. The factor nominal_dep_mod has seven levels, and I am contrasting possible extensions with the reference level *na* (no extension). 

The GLMMs for *unter* and *mit* share the factor nominal_dep_mod, but they differ in the other fixed effects (partly because other fixed effects are relevant, and partly, as in the case of the interpretation of the prepositions, because the interpretations of the prepositions simply differ, see the models below). 

I would like to compare the odds ratios for nominal_dep_mod. If I just compare them, then the results are what I would expect from looking into the data: for one of the prepositions one level of nominal_dep_mod has a much stronger influence than for the other preposition: an odds ratio of 64 vs. an odds ratio of 4, while the other levels are on a par. This level is rc, i.e. extension by a relative clause. The odds ratio of 64 holds for *unter*, so that the presence of a relative clause makes the absence of a determiner very unlikely. For *mit*, it is only 4.  

My perhaps somewhat basic question is: Given the two models, can I conclude from comparing the odds ratios across models that the influence of nominal_dep_mod == rc is much stronger for *unter*, and much weaker for *mit*, although the other factors (random and fixed) differ? From my understanding of GLM(M)s, nothing speaks against this interpretation, but you'll never know ... 

I have added the two calls as well as the xtabs for nominal_dep_mod for reference (the feature names are a crude mix of German and English).

Thanks a lot.

With kind regards

Tibor

Hi all,

I have a question concerning correlated random effects. Following Barr et al., I fitted my model with a maximal random effect structure:

e1=glmer(Response~cGroup*cAccent+(1|Subject)+(cGroup*cAccent+1|Item),E1,family="binomial")

However, the model failed to converge. So I next removed the correlation between item slopes and item intercept.

e1b=glmer(Response~cGroup*cAccent+(1|Subject)+(cGroup*cAccent+0|Item)+(1|Item),E1,family="binomial")

I hope the above is the right way of doing it in the new glmer.

This looks good to me!

The model output suggests that there were strong correlations among the random slopes; and also, the variance for cAccent and the interaction item slope seemed to be very small.

I wonder whether it matters to have highly correlated random effects. I seem to have read that these may cause problems. If they do, how to remedy this?

My understanding is that there may be concerns about high correlations among random effects as sometimes being a symptom of uncertainty in the estimate of the random effects covariance matrix, which the z statistic won’t reflect.  In general, however, large positive or negative correlations among random effects can reflect structure in one’s data and I would certainly recommend against taking out random correlations on the basis that they’re close to ±1 when they’re included in the model!

I’d suggest that you confirm your fixed-effects inferences with the likelihood ratio test, which should be more robust to these kinds of issues.

Also, is it OK to get rid of random slopes with near-zero variances (sounds anti-Barr though).

Well, “OK” is a relative term: the smaller the true variance of the random slope for predictor X, the less anti-conservative inferences about the fixed effect of X will be if the random slope is omitted.

Keep in mind, however, that what counts as small variance depends on the scale of X.  If you’re using sum coding for Group and Accent, then none of your variances count as “near-zero”.  I’d want to see a standard deviation well below 0.1 before I started thinking about it as potentially “near-zero” for a mixed logit model where the predictors are sum-coded.

Finally, if what you really care about is getting p-values for your fixed effects, I don’t see any compelling reason for you to get rid of any of your random slopes.

Best & hope this helps,

Roger

messages.body_plain:
I'd like to follow up to Roger Levy's response with another correlated
random effects question.

I want to test whether two methods of calculating lexical competition
(method1 and method2) each predict unique variance in word recognition
accuracy. The two methods are highly correlated, but are different in
theoretically interesting ways.

I can generate models that include one method each and then a model that
includes both methods and use a likelihood test to evaluate whether the
model with both is a better fit than the models with only one, as below
(omitting random slopes here for simplicity)

m1 = glmer (accuracy ~  *method1* + (1|participants) + (1|items), data,
family = binomial)
m2 = glmer (accuracy ~  *method2* + (1|participants) + (1|items), data,
family = binomial)
m1.2 = glmer (accuracy ~  *method1 + **method2* + (1|participants) + (1|
items), data, family = binomial)

anova(m1, m1.2)
anova(m2, m1.2)

The anovas tell me whether m1.2 provides a better fit than m1 or m2 alone,
but I'm also interested in the direction of the effects when both are in
the model (that is, are method1 and method2 pulling in the same
direction?). However, my understanding is that I can't trust the signs of
the estimates in m1.2, given the degree of collinearity.

How can I determine the direction of the relationship between two collinear
variables and the dependent measure? I'm aware of the residualizing
technique to make the two methods orthogonal before entering them, but Wurm
& Fisicaro
<http://clas.wayne.edu/Multimedia/wurm/files/Wurm%20%26%20Fisicaro%20%282014%29.pdf>
have raised good objections to that method.

Many thanks for your input!

Best,
Julia

messages.body_plain:
Dear list members,

I am using lmer4 package to run linear mixed-effects models on the data
from a sentence comprehension experiment. In this experiment, subjects were
required to read a sentence and answer a following comprehension question.
Thus, we have collected both question answering time data, and question
answering accuracy data. The models that I constructed for RT data and
accuracy data were as follow (both A and B are within-subject variables):

model.RT <- lmer(RT ~A*B + (1+A*B|subject) + (1+A*B|item), data = question)
model.accuracy <- lmer (accuracy~A*B + (1+A*B|subject) + (1+A*B|item), data
= question, family = "binomial")

However, the independent variables had different effects on the RT data and
accuracy data. When we run a simple correlation between the accuracy and
RT-question (averaged across items for each subject), there was no
correlation. I am wondering whether anyone has developed a method for using
both RT and accuracy as dependent measure, simultaneously (like MANOVA -
though not sure how that would work, given logistic regression for accuracy
and not RT) or in some other fashion in combining accuracy and RT measures.

Thanks a lot!

Best,
Yingying

messages.body_plain:
I don't do Manova, but I have similar data quite often. Stop reading
now if you really want an answer to the original question in the
subject line.

For the last 30 years (beginning in print with my 1986 paper with
Badgio and Gaskins, in my web site), following earlier arguments of
others, I have argued that this situation can be seen as the result of
two orthogonal dimensions: ability and reflection/impulsivity
(R/I). Ability increases accuracy and reduces RT. R/I increases
accuracy and increases RT. My general procedure is to convert both
measures to z scores and combine them, either adding or subtracting
depending on what I want. For RT, I usually average the logs of
individual responses before getting the z score for each
subject. (Thus, I use the geometric mean.)

Depending on the task, the correlation between RT and accuracy can be
be positive or negative. For the R/I measure, things work best if the
correlation is positive, and for the ability measure, the
opposite. For items like those in the Raven's Matrices, the
correlation is usually positive.

Clearly there are fancier ways to do this. The relative weight of the
two components depends on variation within the sample of subjects. You
might, instead of using raw z scores, correct them for the relative
reliabilities of the two measures, so that you get equal-weighted true
scores instead of observed scores. I have not bothered to do that. The
relative weights will still depend on the subjects, and I don't know
how to avoid that.

I suppose the point of a Manova would be that you could test overall
significance of both measures. But there are other ways to do that.

Jon

messages.body_plain:
Dear Yingying,

if I understand your question correctly, you are wondering whether models
in R exist that allow you to build in two dependents. I think a good place
to start with that is Gelman and Hill (2006) as well as the Crawley's
(2007) R book. It might be easier to first look at Baayen's handbook (2006)
'Exploratory Data Analysis'. For starters, I would question your initial
assumptions. In other words, why are you looking at two dependents instead
of one? Why are you running a correlation between the two dependents? What
are your hypothesis? How do the results from either the MANOVA or the
correlation help you validate or invalidate your hypothesis or any other
assumption underpinning your study?

You might be getting yourself into unknown territory, statistically
speaking, when in fact you don't need to. Generally, in most
psycholinguistic experiments, we use two distinct dependents to answer
different questions or test distinct aspects of the data we elicit. In this
sense, I'm not sure why you expect the two to correlate. You may find that
RT and accuracy are inversely proportional in one scenario (i.e. those who
read faster have better comprehension), but directly proportional in
another (i.e. those who read slower have better comprehension). This again
boils down to what exactly you intend to answer.

A few minor issues.

1, model.accuracy <- lmer (accuracy~A*B + (1+A*B|subject) + (1+A*B|item),
data = question, family = "binomial") will not work because you need to run
glmer not lmer for binomial data, at least last time I used it.

2. is accuracy a binary dependent? How many responses do you have? Is it
just correct and incorrect or were there 3 or more answers?

Point 2 is especially relevant, as you mentioned, because it calls into
question the very nature of the model you wish to build, since your
mathematical space would be including very different equations, linear and
non-linear (i.e. logistic) regression.

Hope this helps,

Francesco

Hi all,

Thank you all for the reply! I will look into Loeys, Rosseel, and Baten
(2011)'s model, and the book chapters recommended.

In previous ANAOVA analysis, I do tried calculating the composite score for
both logRT and accuracy, as suggested by Dr. Baron (thank you very much for
the detailed discussion). I agreed that there could be two orthogonal
dimensions, and they affect RT and accuracy differently. However, since we
are making use of each single trial data in the mixed-effect model, it
seemed unlikely to calculate the composite score for RT/Accuracy. That's
why I have to think about doing multivariate ANOVA analysis.

I did not make specific hypothesis about the direction of the correlation
between accuracy and RT, which is not the focus of my current project. It
did not affect our prediction whether the correlation between RT and
accuracy was negative, none, or positive, and of course this could be task-
or ability-dependent. I get into this issue because I found that our
experimental manipulation seemed having different influence on accuracy and
RT data, which was less expected. The factor (e.g. semantic complexity)
that affected RT data did not affected accuracy data. Though both measures
are reliable, and there was no floor or ceiling effect. There were studies
on WM (e.g. Unsworth et al.), decision making (e.g. Baron et al.) and
vision, which suggested that it is necessary to think about RT and accuracy
data separately. However, I did not see very much discussion about this in
the sentence reading experiment. Please let me know if anyone had some
thoughts or similar issues like this.

Thanks to all!

Best,
Yingying

However, my understanding is that I can't trust the signs of the estimates in m1.2, given the degree of collinearity.

> How can I determine the direction of the relationship between two collinear variables and the dependent measure? I'm aware of the residualizing technique to make the two methods orthogonal before entering them, but Wurm & Fisicaro have raised good objections to that method.

To answer your query, I’m going to pose a counter-query: what question is it that you want your regression model to answer?  In your model m1.2, the interpretation of the regression coefficient for x1 is, what is the effect on y as the value of x1 changes while the value of x2 is held constant?  (And likewise for x2, mutatis mutandis.)  As Wurm & Fisicaro point out, replacing x1 with a residual from a regression on x2 (e.g., creating x1.res <- resid(lm(x1 ~ x2)) and then using the formula y ~ x1.res + x2) does not change the interpretation of the regression weight for x1, though it *does* change the interpretation of the regression weight for x2.

So, if the regression coefficients in m1.2 don’t have the interpretation that you’re looking for, what interpretation *are* you looking for?

Best & I hope this helps!

Roger

Hi all,

Roger, I had some vague memory of someone offering similar advice before,
and the nearest I can find is  this post by Ben Boker on R-sig-ME

https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-sig-mixed-models/2012q2/018251.html

To quote the post

 "This is a very common situation, and a bit of a tough call (I
haven't seen much in the way of formal, rigorously tested guidance for
this situation.)  What glmer is telling you is essentially that you
really don't have enough data to fit two separate random effects

Bolker offers a number of  solutions, but I think the first two are
pretty common in practice:

"1. You have no _a priori_ way of knowing that the correlation
*is* exactly zero (if you had enough data, you would almost certainly
find that there was a non-zero correlation between these terms);
you shouldn't be doing 'sacrificial' or stepwise removal of terms.
Keep the more complex model.

  2. You should be trying to select the 'minimal adequate' model; in
particular, overfitting the model (including zero and/or perfectly
correlated terms) is more likely to lead to numeric problems, so it's
better to try to reduce the model until all the terms can be uniquely
estimated.  (This is the approach suggested in Bolker et al 2008
_Trends in Ecology and Evolution_)"


I'm never quite certain as to how to proceed in this type of case.
Given that when there is a numeric problem, I typically proceed by
removing correlation terms, it might seem consistent to follow
approach (2). Basically, you are treating perfect correlations as a
numerical problem that just happen not to meet lme4's optimization
diagnostics. I guess the trade-off here is whether you think that is
more likely to create issues with your other parameter estimates than
forcing 0 correlations between random effect terms.


mG

> Hi all,

> Roger, I had some vague memory of someone offering similar advice before, and the nearest I can find is  this post by Ben Boker on R-sig-ME 
> 
> https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-sig-mixed-models/2012q2/018251.html
> 
> To quote the post
>  "This is a very common situation, and a bit of a tough call (I
> haven't seen much in the way of formal, rigorously tested guidance for
> this situation.)  What glmer is telling you is essentially that you
> really don't have enough data to fit two separate random effects
> 
> Bolker offers a number of  solutions, but I think the first two are pretty common in practice:
> "1. You have no _a priori_ way of knowing that the correlation
> *is* exactly zero (if you had enough data, you would almost certainly
> find that there was a non-zero correlation between these terms);
> you shouldn't be doing 'sacrificial' or stepwise removal of terms.
> Keep the more complex model.
> 
> 
>   2. You should be trying to select the 'minimal adequate' model; in
> particular, overfitting the model (including zero and/or perfectly
> correlated terms) is more likely to lead to numeric problems, so it's
> better to try to reduce the model until all the terms can be uniquely
> estimated.  (This is the approach suggested in Bolker et al 2008
> _Trends in Ecology and Evolution_)"
> 
> 
> I'm never quite certain as to how to proceed in this type of case. Given that when there is a numeric problem, I typically proceed by removing correlation terms, it might seem consistent to follow approach (2). Basically, you are treating perfect correlations as a numerical problem that just happen not to meet lme4's optimization diagnostics. I guess the trade-off here is whether you think that is more likely to create issues with your other parameter estimates than forcing 0 correlations between random effect terms.

Thanks Matt.  (Daniel Ezra Johnson also pointed me to this post.)  I note that the example Ben is discussing is a case where there’s not just a perfect correlation, there also seems to be a a very small standard deviation in the random slope (though what the nature of the data are that particular case is hard to figure out once you start to dig deeper into the thread).  If the standard deviation of the random slope is small, then it will be difficult for lme4 to estimate the correlation parameter with high confidence because the specific values that the subject-specific slopes take on simply doesn’t affect the data likelihood much.  And for that reason, another point Ben makes in the thread also applies:

 "5. If you are most interested in inference on the fixed-effect terms, I doubt it matters -- my guess is that these two models give nearly identical fixed-effect estimates.”

Bumping up a notch, I think that the critical point here that makes Ben’s arguments applicable is the fact that the random slope standard deviation is very small.  Having a ±1 correlation parameter isn’t sufficient cause, in my view.  This is because when the correlated random effects (e.g., intercept and slope) are of appreciable size, models where the correlation parameter is forced to zero are simply very different models than those in which the correlation parameter is free and gets fit to ±1, and when you get a ±1 correlation parameter estimate the model is probably a better fit to the data than a zero-correlation model.  Furthermore, as we point out in footnote 6 of Barr et al. (2013), once you remove the correlation parameter between the random intercept and the random slope for X (
 or between the random slopes for two different predictors) your model class changes with the coding of X when X is a factor, or with additive transformations of X when X is numeric.  Therefore one needs to proceed with extra caution when removing correlation parameters.

Best

Roger

Hi Stephanie,


The title of your post ('slope') suggests that what you're interested in is regression, not correlation. Regression and correlation analyses provide answers to different, if related, questions, see Figure 2 (and main text) of

http://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0069172


If it's regression slopes, rather than correlation coefficients, you're interested in, you can probably run a regression analysis with an interaction term between one 'dependent' variable (modelled as a predictor in this model) and the independent variable (DV2 ~ DV1 + IV + DV1:IV). It may be a bit confusing to model a 'dependent' variable as a predictor, but the interaction term should give you the answer you're looking for (if it's slopes you're interested in).


I don't really know what you mean with "I am doing this test within each subject." Do you have two DV2s and two DV1s measurements for each subject, one each in each condition? In that case I don't know how to compare the correlation coefficients (if it's correlation coefficient you're really interested in).

But if you're interested in regression slopes, I think a mixed model (with subjects as a hierarchical level) would do.


HTH,

Jan

If you are interested in comparing correlations, then indeed paired.r
is a good way to do it. It isn't clear from your question whether the
different dependent variables (DVs) are varied between subjects or
within, but it doesn't matter since paired.r has tests for both
independent (between) and dependent (within) correlations.

If you are interested in slopes, as Jan Vanhove suggests based on your
subject line, then, if the two DVs are between subjects, you could
re-name your two DVs so that they are a single variable, include a
dummy variable to indicate the DV used, and look for an interaction
between the IV and the dummy in predicting the new DV.

If the DVs are withing subject, then another alternative for slopes
(not correlations) is: (DV1-DV2) ~ IV.

I fear that Jan's approach will give different results depending on
which DV you put where. For example, try it with
IV <- c(1,2,3,4,20)
DV1 <- c(1,2,3,4,5)
DV2 <- c(1,4,9,16,25)

Jon

Dear Yingying et al,

sorry to get to this so late. Multivariate models (which your intended case
is an example of) can be run in R. Multivariate models are a generalization
of MANOVA.

Mixed/Multilevel Multivariate models can also be run, for example, via
mcmcglmm. It's quite a bit more complicated than using lme4, since you need
to specify priors and check convergences of the sampling chains.

A tutorial for the multinomial case is provided on the HLP Lab blog at
https://hlplab.wordpress.com/2009/05/07/multinomial-random-effects-models-in-r/
.

There's also a poster and an (outdated) manuscript by Austin Frank, Anne
Pier Salverda, Mike Tanenhaus and me from, I think, 2009, where we combine
the modeling of a three-way multinomial outcome and a normally distributed
outcome (fixation locations in a VWP paradigm plus the fixation durations).
That model subsumes what you need to model accuracy and reaction times
together.

hth,

Florian

messages.body_plain:
Stephanie,

perhaps this is relevant, too: the multivariate approach described in my
reply to the MANOVA question also extends to two continuous dependent
variables. An example of non-mixed (ordinary) bivariate normal regression
is given in Lecture 3 of a class I taught at the 2013 LSA:

http://wiki.bcs.rochester.edu/HlpLab/LSA2013Regression

I used VGAM for that back then, which *I think* can be extended to a mixed
models. In any case, I'm pretty sure that mcmcglmm can also be used for
this case.

I'm not sure whether this is what you need, but it does provide an estimate
of the effect of the correlation between two dependent variables while
estimating the effect of a fixed effect on both of those variables,
which *sounds
*like what you were looking for?

Florian
